## Solution

**Claim.** No analytic extension of $f(x)=|x|$ to $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ exists.

**Proof.**

Suppose, for contradiction, that there exists a holomorphic function $F:\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb{C}$ such that $F(x)=|x|$ for every $x\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$.

Consider the holomorphic function $G(z)=z$ on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$. On the open ray $(0,\infty)\subset\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ we have $|x|=x$, hence
$$F(x)=|x|=x=G(z)\big|_{z=x}\quad\text{for all }x\in(0,\infty).$$

The domain $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ is connected (it is path-connected, hence connected) and open, so it is a region in the sense required by the **identity theorem**. The set $(0,\infty)$ is contained in $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ and has an accumulation point in $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ — for instance, $1\in(0,\infty)$ is a limit point of $(0,\infty)$ and $1\neq 0$.

Since $F$ and $G$ are both holomorphic on the region $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ and they agree on the set $(0,\infty)$ which has a limit point inside $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$, the identity theorem forces
$$F(z)=G(z)=z\quad\text{for all }z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}.$$

Now evaluate at $x=-1\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$. On one hand, by the assumed agreement with $|x|$,
$$F(-1)=|-1|=1.$$
On the other hand, by the identity theorem conclusion $F(z)=z$,
$$F(-1)=-1.$$
This is a contradiction: $1\neq -1$.

The contradiction shows that our supposition was false. Therefore **there is no holomorphic (analytic) function on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ that agrees with $|x|$ on $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$**.

**Remark on why the puncture at $0$ does not help.** One might hope that removing the non-analytic point $0$ would allow an extension. It does not, because the obstruction is global, not local: the two real-analytic pieces of $|x|$ — namely $x$ on $(0,\infty)$ and $-x$ on $(-\infty,0)$ — extend to the holomorphic functions $z$ and $-z$ respectively, and these two extensions disagree on every point of $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ (they differ by a sign). Since $(0,\infty)$ already has accumulation points in $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$, the identity theorem rigidly forces any extension to be $z$ everywhere, which is incompatible with the value $-x$ required on $(-\infty,0)$. Removing $0$ only disconnects the two real pieces from each other on the *real* line, but $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ remains connected as a complex domain, so the identity theorem still binds the two sides together. $\blacksquare$
